analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a national sales tax and abolishes the IRS.
analysis.headline: The bill to replace all federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Tax Act would repeal every federal income tax, corporate tax, payroll tax, and estate tax, and replace them with a 23% national sales tax on nearly everything people buy, collected mostly by the states. Households would get a monthly rebate check sized to the poverty line to offset tax on basic necessities. The IRS would be defunded, and the whole plan would automatically shut off unless Congress also passed a constitutional amendment repealing the income tax within seven years.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy households gain the most: they would pay no tax on investment income, no estate or gift tax, and no income tax at all, while the tax burden moves to consumption. High earners keep far more of every paycheck. Low-income households do get help, in the form of a monthly rebate covering the sales tax up to the poverty line, and state governments gain a new fee and a central role collecting the tax.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the entire federal income tax, corporate income tax, payroll and self-employment taxes, and the estate and gift tax, replacing them all with a single national sales tax starting at 23% in 2017.
Exempts purchases made for investment purposes from the sales tax, so wealth held for appreciation or income production would never be taxed, while purchases for personal consumption would be.
Eliminates the estate and gift tax entirely, removing the only federal tax on very large inheritances.
Shuts off all funding for IRS operations after fiscal year 2019, ending the agency that audits and enforces the current income tax.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers. Everyone would pay 23% tax on new goods and services — food, rent, cars, clothes, utilities — while wages and investment returns go untaxed. Because lower- and middle-income households spend most or all of their income, and wealthy households spend only a fraction of theirs, the tax would fall proportionally hardest on ordinary workers even after the monthly poverty-line rebate. Social Security and Medicare would also lose their dedicated payroll-tax funding and depend instead on annual general-revenue appropriations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary consumers, especially low and middle incomes

drawbacks.text: The 23% sales tax applies to almost everything a family buys, and because low- and middle-income households spend nearly all of their income on consumption while the wealthy spend only a slice of theirs, the tax shift would raise the relative burden on working families even with the rebate.

The monthly rebate is not automatic: every family must register each year with the tax authority, listing Social Security numbers and certifying every member is a lawful resident; a missed registration cuts off the payments, and no family member who is incarcerated six months or longer counts.

Social Security and Medicare would lose their dedicated payroll-tax funding and rely on annual allocations from general revenue, making their financing subject to yearly congressional budget fights rather than an earmarked tax.
The bill's own rate formula allows the combined rate to change after 2017, so the sales tax rate would not be locked at 23%.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplification argument is real: filing income taxes would end, and state revenue agencies that already run sales taxes would do the collecting. But the trade is a wholesale shift of federal taxation away from income and inheritances and onto consumption. The rebate cushions the poorest households at the poverty line, yet between the poverty line and the top, working families would pay a larger share of their income in federal tax while households living on accumulated wealth would pay close to none, and the estate tax — paid only on multi-million-dollar inheritances — disappears outright. The costs fall disproportionately on the people the simplification is sold to.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2015 and sat there for the rest of the Congress, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Jerry Moran introduced the Fair Tax Act of 2015 in the Senate on January 13, 2015; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
Six Republican senators signed on as cosponsors; no Democrats did.
No further action of any kind was recorded — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary households are better off that it died: the existing income tax system, under which higher earners and large estates pay federal tax, stayed in place. The tax-preparation industry and the IRS also kept their roles.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working households; the estate tax survived

for.name: Sen. Jerry Moran
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. David Perdue and Johnny Isakson
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as original cosponsors.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: The Finance Committee, which he chaired, took no action after the bill was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the entire two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to measure, but support was entirely Republican: the sponsor and all 6 cosponsors were Senate Republicans, and no Democrat signed on.

industries.note: Investment income would go untaxed and the estate and gift tax would be repealed, while the replacement sales tax falls on consumption, which makes up a much larger share of ordinary families' income. The gains flow in one direction: up.

Purchases made for investment purposes are exempt from the tax, and capital gains, dividends, and interest face no tax at all under the bill. The return on wealth would be the only major form of income untouched by federal tax.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: With the income tax repealed and IRS operations defunded after FY2019, the industry built around annual income-tax filing loses its market. Some of its work would migrate to sales-tax compliance for sellers.

Sellers would collect a large new federal tax and face registration, segregated-account, and bond requirements, but they would receive an administration credit of at least $200 per month (or 0.25% of tax remitted) and would no longer withhold or remit payroll taxes.

States that keep a sales tax could sign up as administering states, collecting the federal tax for a fee of 0.25% of what they remit. States without a sales tax, or that decline, would have the Treasury collect directly.
The bill contains special rules for gaming sponsors and wagers, and taxes gambling activity as a service, replacing the current federal wagering excise regime.
